title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography
body:
Same protocols, different [[Group]]. [[Diffie-Hellman]], [[ElGamal]], and
[[Digital Signature|DSA]] are all written in terms of a [[Cyclic Group]] and a hard
[[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] in it; elliptic curve cryptography swaps $\mathbb{Z}_p^*$ for the
points on a curve and changes nothing else. **The payoff is key size**: 256 bits of curve gives the
security of 3072 bits of finite field.

## The group

An elliptic curve over a [[Finite Field]] $\mathbb{F}_p$ is the solution set of

$$y^2 = x^3 + ax + b$$

together with a point at infinity $\mathcal{O}$. The remarkable fact, and the reason the subject
exists, is that **those points form an abelian group**, with $\mathcal{O}$ as the identity.

The operation is geometric. To add $P$ and $Q$, draw the line through them; a cubic meets a line in
exactly three points, so there is a third intersection, and $P + Q$ is its reflection in the
$x$-axis. Doubling uses the tangent line instead. Over a finite field there is no picture, but the
formulas obtained from the geometry are just rational functions and they still satisfy the group
axioms.

```
P + Q + R = O  when P, Q, R are collinear
P + Q = -R     reflect the third point

-P is P with y negated
P + (-P) = O
```

Associativity is the one axiom that is not obvious, and proving it properly is the whole reason
elliptic curves are a research subject rather than a trick. Everything else falls out of the
construction. This is [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] used at full strength: a group axiom check on an object
with no resemblance to the integers, and every group theorem then applies for free, including
[[Lagrange's Theorem]] on the order of the point group.

## Scalar multiplication is the one-way function

Repeated addition, $kP = P + P + \dots + P$, computed by double-and-add in $O(\log k)$ steps,
exactly as square-and-multiply computes $g^k$ in [[Modular Arithmetic]]. Going backwards is the
**elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem**: given $P$ and $kP$, find $k$.

| Multiplicative group | Elliptic curve group |
|---|---|
| $g^k$ | $kP$ |
| square-and-multiply | double-and-add |
| DLP | ECDLP |
| Diffie-Hellman | ECDH |
| DSA | ECDSA |

The private key is a scalar $k$; the public key is the point $kP$.

## Why the keys are smaller

**Index calculus does not work on curves.** In $\mathbb{Z}_p^*$ that algorithm gives a
sub-exponential attack, because integers factor into small primes and you can build relations out
of a factor base. There is no analogue of "small prime" among curve points, so the best known
attack on a well-chosen curve is generic Pollard's rho at $O(\sqrt{n})$, and the key only has to be
twice the security level.

| Security level | RSA / finite-field DH | Elliptic curve |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 112 bits | 2048 | 224 |
| 128 bits | 3072 | 256 |
| 256 bits | 15360 | 512 |

Smaller keys mean less bandwidth in every handshake and far less work per operation, which is why
ECDHE and Ed25519 are the modern defaults and why constrained devices use nothing else.

**Curves must be chosen carefully rather than generated randomly.** Supersingular and anomalous
curves have efficiently solvable ECDLP, so real deployments use named curves (P-256, Curve25519)
whose parameters have been verified. Curve25519 was designed specifically to make the
implementation hard to get wrong, which is a different and equally important kind of security.

[[Post-Quantum Cryptography|Shor's algorithm]] breaks ECDLP as thoroughly as it breaks factoring,
and the shorter keys are no defence at all: a quantum computer needs *fewer* qubits for a 256-bit
curve than for a 2048-bit RSA modulus. Elliptic curves are the current best answer and not the
long-term one.
